title: 1000 Layer Networks for Self-Supervised RL: Scaling Depth Can Enable New G

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states: 'Note additionally that the parameter count scales linearly with width but quadratically with depth.' This is incorrect. In standard fully-connected networks with constant width, the number of parameters scales linearly with the number of layers (depth) and quadratically with the width. The statement is reversed, which misrepresents the scaling properties and undermines the argument that depth scaling is more parameter-efficient.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 9 caption and surrounding text in Section 4.5
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper uses L2-distance \(Q(s,a,g) = \|\phi(s,a) - \psi(g)\|_2\) to visualize and interpret the Q-function, but the contrastive RL algorithm's critic is defined as a dot-product \(f(s,a,g) = \phi(s,a)^\top \psi(g)\). The actual Q-values used for policy optimization are based on the dot product, not the L2 distance. Presenting L2 distance as the Q-function is misleading and misrepresents what the network has learned.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.4, paragraph 'Scaling the Actor vs. Critic Networks', discussion of Figure 6
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper claims that 'coordinated depth increases resulting in an average 30% improvement over critic-only or actor-only scaling across tasks.' The table in Figure 6 shows that when comparing the best joint scaling with critic-only scaling (actor depth fixed at 4) in the three environments, the improvements are approximately 5.6% (Humanoid), 23.6% (Ant Big Maze), and 5.7% (Arm Push Easy), averaging around 11.6%, not 30%. The claimed 30% improvement is not supported by the presented numbers and appears inflated.
